\chapter{People under one roof}
\label{ch:zh-family-six}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can understand, say, read and write six HSK Level 1 people-and-family words, building \zh{儿子}, \zh{女儿} and \zh{家人} only after their spoken meanings and component characters are secure.}

Six family words pass separate listening, speaking, reading and no-model writing checks; pinyin cannot compensate for an unread character, and a strong skill cannot compensate for a weak one.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[rén]{\zh{人} — a person}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-ren}



\begin{quote}
Write the two-stroke figure, then say \textbf{wǒ} — I.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{人}} — \emph{rén} — \textbf{person}
\end{quote}

Hear the rising tone first. Say \emph{rén}. Now read the character you already know. The meaning is singular here: one person. Number comes from context or another word; the character itself does not grow a plural ending.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say \textbf{person} in Mandarin. Read \textbf{\zh{人}}. Cover it, wait five seconds, and write it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nǚ]{\zh{女} — female, woman}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-nu}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{person}, then write the three-stroke left half of \zh{好}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{女}} — \emph{nǚ} — \textbf{female; woman}
\end{quote}

Say it low: \emph{nǚ}. The rounded vowel is the same written \textbf{ü} you met in the character lesson. On its own, \zh{女} labels female gender; it is not a polite way to call out to a woman. Here you are learning the word for reading and building.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read \textbf{\zh{女}}, cover it, and write it from the meaning cue \textbf{female}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary entry 152}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[érzi]{Hear \emph{érzi} — son}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-hear-erzi}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{person}, then \textbf{female}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{érzi} — \textbf{son}
\end{quote}

Hear two beats: rising \emph{ér}, then a short, light \emph{zi}. Say the whole word once from the meaning. Keep the characters covered; the new first shape comes next.

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ér]{\zh{儿} — fall, then bend and hook}

\label{lesson:ZH-W12-er}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{son}, then write \zh{人}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{儿}}
\end{quote}

Two strokes. First a short fall down-left. Then start high on the right, descend, bend right along the floor, and hook upward \textbf{without lifting}. Unlike \zh{人}, the two strokes do not meet at the top.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\zh{儿}} once. Copy it once. Point to the bend that keeps it apart from \zh{人}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%84\%BF.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{儿}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{儿子} — son on the page}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-erzi}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{son}, then write \zh{儿} and \zh{子} separately.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{儿子}} — \emph{érzi} — \textbf{son}
\end{quote}

The first syllable rises. The second is light. Both characters carry child meanings, but the whole word—not either character alone—is the ordinary kinship word \textbf{son}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\zh{儿子}} once while saying \emph{ér-zi}. Then read it once without pinyin.

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nǚ'ér]{Hear \emph{nǚ'ér} — daughter}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-hear-nuer}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{female}, then \textbf{son}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{nǚ'ér} — \textbf{daughter}
\end{quote}

Say two clear syllables: low \emph{nǚ}, rising \emph{ér}. The apostrophe only keeps the vowel boundary visible in pinyin. It is not a pause and not part of the Chinese writing.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary entry 153}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{女儿} — daughter on the page}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-nuer}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{daughter}, then write \zh{女} and \zh{儿} separately.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{女儿}} — \emph{nǚ'ér} — \textbf{daughter}
\end{quote}

Nothing is hidden: \zh{女} gives female and \zh{儿} gives child. Read the two characters without the pinyin, then say the whole word without a pause.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\zh{女儿}}, cover it, wait five seconds, and write it from \textbf{daughter}.

\section[jiā]{Hear \emph{jiā} — home, family}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-hear-jia}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{daughter}, then \textbf{son}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{jiā} — \textbf{home; family}
\end{quote}

Hold the pitch high and level: \emph{jiā}. The word can name the household place or the family belonging to it. Keep the character covered; it has ten strokes, and the next lesson gives them to you in two familiar-sized pieces.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary entry 86}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jiā]{\zh{家} — roof first, body second}

\label{lesson:ZH-W12-jia}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{home}, then write the roof from \zh{字} and the whole character \zh{字}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{宀}} + \textbf{\zh{豕}} $\to$ \textbf{\zh{家}}
\end{quote}

Finish the three-stroke roof first. Under it, write the lower body from its top horizontal through the centre curve, three left-falling strokes, and the long right-falling finish. Ten strokes; nine lifts.

The old lower component is \zh{豕}, livestock. That decomposition is real history and a useful shape boundary. It is not a claim that a present-day home or family is defined by an animal.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\zh{家}} once. Copy it once, saying \textbf{roof}, then \textbf{body}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%AE\%B6.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{家}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{家} — home on the page}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-jia}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{home or family}, then write \zh{宀}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{家}} — \emph{jiā} — \textbf{home; family}
\end{quote}

Read it once without pinyin. The high line over \emph{ā} records first tone; the character records no tone mark at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Copy \textbf{\zh{家}} once from the model. Name the roof before you write the lower body.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary entry 86}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jiārén]{Hear \emph{jiārén} — family members}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-hear-jiaren}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{home or family}, then \textbf{person}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{jiārén} — \textbf{family members; family}
\end{quote}

You already own both sounds: \emph{jiā} + \emph{rén}. The compound names the people of the home. Say it once from the meaning before looking at either character.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://hsk.cn-bj.ufileos.com/3.0/\%E6\%96\%B0\%E7\%89\%88HSK\%E8\%80\%83\%E8\%AF\%95\%E5\%A4\%A7\%E7\%BA\%B21219.pdf}{Official HSK 3.0 syllabus, Level 1 vocabulary entry 87}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{家人} — the people of the home}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-jiaren}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{family members}, then write \zh{家} and \zh{人} separately.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{家人}} — \emph{jiārén} — \textbf{family members; family}
\end{quote}

Read from the characters: home + person. The word is plural by meaning here, but Mandarin adds no plural ending to \zh{人}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\zh{家人}}, cover it, wait five seconds, and write it from \textbf{family}.

\section[Practice]{Payoff — six family words in four skills}

\label{lesson:ZH-C12-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{name}, then write \zh{儿} and \zh{家} without a model.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
1. \textbf{Listening:} hear six words in mixed order and choose each meaning. 2. \textbf{Speaking:} produce all six from meaning cards, with tones audible. 3. \textbf{Reading:} read the six character cards without pinyin. 4. \textbf{Writing:} hear all six and write them without a model.

Pass each skill separately. If one misses, repair that skill and retry only that part. This is a family vocabulary map, not yet a full family-description task.
